extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patentees, and patent attorneys drafting complete patent specifications (practitioners preparing/assessing UK-style specifications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing a complete patent specification so it fairly, fully and intelligibly discloses the invention and how to carry it into effect. Focuses on sufficiency of disclosure, materials/process details, claim scope, and what must be communicated to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate description of ingredients and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Ingredients must be accurately described; proportions, quantities, times, temperatures, and the like, so far as they are respectively material, must be stated, precisely if it can be done, approximately if that only is possible; whilst the needful processes and operations must be fully communicated and clearly unfolded. These things should be taken in proper order, and expressed in perspicuous language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precise numerical values where material (or state approximate values if precision impossible). Describe processes step-by-step in order. Use clear, perspicuous language so a skilled worker can follow without undue experimentation. (General principle stated at start of the chapter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and fair statement of what the invention is and how to do it
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification ought to contain a full description of the way in which it is to be done. The patentee ought to state in his specification the precise way of doing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not enable the invention to be carried out by following it, the patentee cannot reliably sue for infringement. Case: Morgan v. Seward (address of Baron Alderton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention everything essential to carrying the invention into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification ought to mention everything which is essential to the carrying into effect of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit no material components or steps without explanation — omissions of essential features (e.g., tempering with tallow, water-tuyeres) have led to invalidation (Liardet v. Johnson; Neilson v. Harford).

rubrics_metrics.name: State quantities/proportions when material
rubrics_metrics.description: When quantities/proportions are material they must be stated; omission of ingredient quantities can render a specification bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention depends on proportions (e.g., mixtures, flour+malt proportions), provide them; failure to do so has resulted in invalid patents (Dr. James fever powders; Pooley bread case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague/general descriptions when claiming broad rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Description must not be vague and general. When a patentee attempts to secure a right of an extensive nature, the description of the process must not be vague and general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sweeping claim requires particular description of how to achieve it; general references (e.g., 'same as ordinary apparatus') are insufficient (Booth v. Kennard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precisely describe materials and avoid overly general class terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification, in describing materials and ingredients required for carrying the invention into effect, must not employ general terms which cover what is unsuitable as well as what is suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you claim a class of materials, identify which members are suitable; you cannot leave the public to test which members work (Turner v. Winter; Stevens v. Keating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim classes containing unsuitable or dangerous members without definition
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed class (e.g., 'earthy sulphites' or 'alkaline and earthy sulphites') contains members that are poisonous or unsuitable, the claim is too wide or vague unless the specification defines the suitable members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either limit the claim to suitable members or expressly identify which within the class are proper (Bailey v. Roberton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial meaning of named articles
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of articles mentioned in a specification must be taken to be used in their ordinary commercial sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trade names/ordinary commercial names where appropriate; courts will construe names by their commercial meaning (Simpson v. Holliday; Sturtz v. De la Rue).

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to give minute details for well‑known shop materials
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not obligatory on a patentee, when referring to materials and ingredients to be used in carrying his invention into effect, to enter into minute details as to such materials and ingredients, if they are known in the shops, and can be readily purchased under the names which he gives them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a material is commercially available and known by name, naming it can suffice (MacKintosh v. Ferron).

rubrics_metrics.name: State most suitable proportions within patentee's knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who takes out a patent for an invention consisting of the use of known materials in new proportions, though bound to state the most suitable proportions within his knowledge, is not bound to limit his claim to the precise proportions recommended by him in his specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose best-known proportions but claims need not be strictly confined to the exact numbers given; evidence and case law guide boundaries (Patent Type Founding Co. v. Richard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of material description can be a question for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or not a specification describes with sufficient accuracy the material out of which an article is to be made is a question for the jury, where the case is tried before one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual sufficiency (e.g., what kind of 'china' is meant) may be resolved by juries on evidence (Bickford v. Skeives and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the best (most advantageous) method known to you
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is bound to describe the most advantageous method within his knowledge for carrying his invention into effect; and he ought to put the public in possession of his secret in as ample and beneficial a way as he himself uses it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor uses a secret expedient that materially improves manufacture/process (e.g., adding aquafortis), it must be disclosed; concealment can void the patent (Wood v. Zimmer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mislead by describing laborious production of purchasable ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification describes elaborate methods for producing ingredients that are in fact readily purchasable, the public may be misled; the patentee should identify the simplest route if that is what he uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid describing non-essential production methods for known ingredients; show the plainest and easiest way the patentee adopts (Scarn v. Trier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose any circumstances known to you that conduce to advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee knows of any circumstance which conduces to the advantage of his manufacture or process, he is bound to mention it in his specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withhold nothing of importance; known advantageous features must be disclosed (Turner v. Winter, Neilson v. Harford).

rubrics_metrics.name: If multiple methods described, ensure all are possible and avoid stating impossible ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is not bound to explain which of several methods is the most or least advantageous; yet all the methods described by him must be more or less possible, and he is bound to state what methods are possible, and to avoid stating as possible the methods, if any, which are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include descriptions of methods you know to be inoperative; include viable alternatives but need not rank them (Badische Anilin und Soda Fabrik v. Levinstein; Kurtz v. Spence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete specification must include improvements discovered before filing it
rubrics_metrics.description: If between the application and the lodging of the complete specification the inventor discovers that the original invention is capable of material improvement, he is bound to communicate to the public the best information he possesses at the time of lodging the complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the complete specification to convey improvements discovered during the provisional period, but do not add subject matter that extends beyond the original invention (Crompton v. Jenkins; Compton v. Patent Infringement Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additions in complete specification must relate to the original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The additions must strictly relate to the invention as it stood at the date of the application. The introduction of new heads into the specification or an extension of the subject-matter of the original invention will not be permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may incorporate refinements discovered after the provisional filing only insofar as they are within the scope of the originally claimed invention (Penn v. Butler; Haley v. Roberton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need not set forth every possible application of a principle
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor who obtains a patent for the useful application of a principle is not to be called on to set forth every mode of applying it. It is sufficient if he shows some of its useful applications, those applications being the best illustrations of the invention known to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose illustrative, practical applications known to you; but a general claim cannot later cover applications/improvements unknown at the date of specification (Neilson v. Harford; Badische Anilin und Soda Fabrik v. Levinstein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be intelligible to persons of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is to be considered as addressed to persons of ordinary skill and ability, acquainted with the particular subject. It must be intelligible to such persons, and the directions must be such that, by pursuing them, they would produce without difficulty the result which the patentee describes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft with the competent skilled worker in mind—not requiring exceptional scientific genius. Provide enough detail so a careful, competent worker can practise the invention without new invention (Gibson v. Brand; Neilson v. Harford; Hex v. Arkwright).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable performance without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be no necessity to try elaborate experiments in order to ascertain the meaning of the instrument or to accomplish the end promised by the patentee. A specification which casts upon the public the expense and labour of experiments and trial is undoubtedly bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If following the directions as written yields some practical benefit without elaborate trials, that may suffice; but do not leave crucial parameters to be found only by experiment (Rex v. Wheeler; Neilson's Patent; Otto v. Linford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent/correctable errors v. errors discoverable only by experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors which any workman of ordinary skill and experience would perceive and correct will not vitiate a patent if they appear on the face of the specification or drawings; but the proposition is not correct if applied to errors which are discoverable only by experiment and further inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typographical/obvious mistakes that a skilled worker would immediately correct do not invalidate; mistakes that require experimentation to reveal (or that falsely suggest efficacy of inoperative processes) can vitiate the patent (Lord Westbury's observations; Simpson v. Holliday).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not describe processes including wholly ineffectual options as producing the claimed result
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification describes several processes or combinations and affirms they will produce a certain result, and some one of the processes or combinations is wholly ineffectual and useless, the patent will be bad even if the mistake would be at once observed by an ordinary workman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that every method/combo you assert produces the claimed result is actually operative; including an inoperative variant can invalidate the entire specification (Simpson v. Holliday).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify kinds/qualities where variation affects operability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where varieties of a material exist and only certain kinds are suitable (e.g., different kinds of china with differing silica content), the specification must state which kind is to be employed; otherwise experiments would be required and the specification may be ambiguous and inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material properties (grade, composition) affect function, identify the required grade or otherwise describe the material sufficiently to avoid trial-and-error (Weginann v. Corcoran).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical evidence that the specification works can save sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is shown in evidence that the patented article had been made by following the instructions of the specification, the specification may be held sufficient for practical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrable practice by others following the specification is strong evidence of sufficiency; courts will consider practical success (British Dynamite Co. v. Krebs).
